Worth running if the automatic import did not finish, or if history has synced in from another device since. Safe to repeat: counts are matched, not added up.

The common trick is a site that asks you to copy a line and paste it into a terminal or a run box, and what actually landed in the clipboard is malicious code rather than the harmless line you saw on screen. punycodeHelpContent.message:
Punycode is a technical format for domains with special characters. It starts with 'xn--'.

Potential Risk:
The danger arises when a domain looks like it only contains standard English letters (ASCII), but is actually Punycode. This usually means it contains hidden 'look-alike' characters from other languages to impersonate a trusted site.

If the domain characters are in the same language as the website content, then Punycode is expected and likely safe.

linkShortUrlSectionWarning.message: Resolving a short link means actually requesting it and following every hop to the end. Each host along the way sees that request, the final destination included, so it learns your address and that someone followed the link. It is still far less exposure than opening the page, because nothing is rendered and no script on it ever runs, but it is not nothing: a click can be counted, a one-time link can be spent, and a server can act on the request. If a link looks suspicious, not resolving it at all is the safer choice.

antiTamperingSettingsDesc.message: Detects when a page forcibly hides or removes the extension's warnings from this site (i.e. removes the extension's UI from the DOM). If tampering is detected, you'll receive a critical security warning. Some legitimate sites that heavily rebuild their page (especially SPAs or sites with aggressive DOM cleanup) may trigger false alarms – add them to the exclusion list below. Check the address carefully before you add anything. Protection is off for everything on that list, so an excluded site can take Visilant's panel off the page with nothing left to report it. A fake that ends up on the list is exactly the page that would do that.

emailCaveatNoMailbox.message: This check only ever saw the address. It has no way into your mail, so it never learns which server really sent the message or what the message says. Everything above is worth knowing – none of it makes a message safe.
emailCaveatNoMailbox.description: First paragraph of the email caveat: no mailbox integration

emailCaveatReadAddress.message: Once the domain looks right, the name in front of it is what is left, and one swapped character is the whole trick. Do not read the two by eye if you can help it: if an earlier message from this person went somewhere, paste that address into the comparison above and the difference is pointed at for you.
emailCaveatReadAddress.description: Second paragraph: compare the address against an earlier one rather than by eye

emailCaveatSenderHacked.message: An address you know is still not the end of it, because a real sender can be hacked. What the message asks you to do is the better question.
emailCaveatSenderHacked.description: Third paragraph: a genuine sender can be compromised

emailCaveatLinks.message: A link or a QR code out of the message can be pasted into the field above, and it is worth doing when the link claims to be somewhere you already use. Whether it really is that site is the one question this extension can answer. A name you have never seen before it cannot judge at all, and neither can you by looking, so put that one through {virustotal-url} or {urlscan} instead.
emailCaveatLinks.description: Fourth paragraph: when checking a link here helps, and when it does not

emailCaveatAttachments.message: Attachments are a different matter: ask someone you trust if you have anybody to ask, and otherwise send the file to {virustotal-file} rather than opening it. If you are in doubt, do not download it at all – some file types can do harm before anyone opens them.
emailCaveatAttachments.description: Fifth paragraph: what to do with an attachment

addressCompareHint.message: Reading an address letter by letter is the advice, and eyes are bad at it. If an earlier message from the same person went somewhere, paste that address here and the difference will be pointed at instead.

welcomeTitle.description: Title of the welcome page shown right after install

welcomeSubtitle.message: One thing was set up for you.

welcomeWhyTitle.description: Heading of the section explaining why the history was imported

welcomeWhyBody.message: Visilant decides what to warn about by comparing a site against the ones you already use. With nothing to compare against it cannot tell your bank from a copy of it, so on an empty profile it either stays quiet when it should not, or flags everything in sight. A warning that appears on every site is a warning you stop reading – and by the time a genuinely dangerous one turns up, it looks exactly like the harmless ones before it. Reading your history once, up front, is what makes the difference between the two mean something.
welcomeWhyBody.description: Explanation of why the history import happens automatically

welcomeStatusReading.description: Shown while the browser history is being read

welcomeStatusSaving.description: Shown while the imported sites are being saved

welcomeStatusDone.message: These sites are now familiar to Visilant and will not be warned about. Everything else still will be.
welcomeStatusDone.description: Shown under the import result numbers

welcomeStatusFailed.message: The import did not finish, so Visilant still treats every site as new. You can run it again.
welcomeStatusFailed.description: Shown when the automatic import failed

welcomeStatusCancelled.message: The import was stopped before it finished. You can run it again.
welcomeStatusCancelled.description: Shown when the import was stopped before finishing

welcomeStatusUnsupported.message: This browser keeps its history to itself, so there was nothing to import. Visilant learns your sites as you visit them, and until it has seen a site it will call it unfamiliar.
welcomeStatusUnsupported.description: Shown when the browser has no history API, as on Firefox for Android

welcomeDetailsRunning.message: Your sites are already counted, and warnings already know them. Filling in first-visit dates and active-day counts now.
welcomeDetailsRunning.description: Shown while the slower detail pass of the import is still running

welcomeKeepOpen.message: Carry on browsing as usual and feel free to close this page – the import runs in the background. Just try not to close the browser itself until it is done. If you do, it saves its place as it goes and picks up where it left off next time you start the browser.
welcomeKeepOpen.description: Hint shown while the import runs, about keeping the browser open

welcomeTabDone.description: Tab title flashed when the import finishes while the user is on another tab

welcomeDetailsFailed.message: The extra pass that fills in first-visit dates did not finish. Your sites are counted either way, so warnings already work. Only those dates are missing.
welcomeDetailsFailed.description: Shown when the detail pass failed but the counting pass succeeded

welcomeRetry.description: Label of the button that runs the import again

welcomeStatSites.description: Unit under the number of imported sites

welcomeStatVisits.description: Unit under the number of imported visits

welcomeSavedTitle.description: Heading of the list of what the import stored

welcomeSavedHostname.message: the host name of the site, such as example.com
welcomeSavedHostname.description: First item of what the import stored

welcomeSavedCount.message: how many times you have been there
welcomeSavedCount.description: Second item of what the import stored

welcomeSavedFirstSeen.message: the date of your earliest recorded visit
welcomeSavedFirstSeen.description: Item of what the import stored: the first visit date

welcomeSavedLastSeen.description: Third item of what the import stored

welcomeSavedActiveDays.message: how many separate days you visited it on
welcomeSavedActiveDays.description: Item of what the import stored: the number of active days

welcomeSavedRetention.message: These numbers only reach as far back as the browser’s own history does. Browsers drop old entries after a while on their own, so a site you have used for years can show far fewer visits and a much later first visit than you would expect. That is the browser’s retention setting rather than a miscount. It also explains why a site you have known for years, but visit rarely, can fall short of the familiarity threshold and trigger a warning. From here on Visilant keeps its own count and misses none of your visits. It simply cannot look backwards, so a gap like that belongs to the early days and closes as you browse.
welcomeSavedRetention.description: Note that the imported numbers only reach as far back as the browser keeps history

welcomeSubtitleNoImport.message: Nothing was read, and nothing had to be.
welcomeSubtitleNoImport.description: Subtitle of the welcome page on a browser that does not share its history

welcomeWhyTitleNoImport.description: Heading of the first welcome section on a browser with no history API

welcomeWhyBodyNoImport.message: Visilant decides what to warn about by comparing a site against the ones you already use. Here there was nothing to start from, so it begins knowing nothing at all. That is worth knowing up front, because for the first while it will call sites unfamiliar that you have used for years – including your bank and your mailbox. It is not wrong, it simply has not seen them yet. Every visit teaches it one, and the warnings thin out on their own.
welcomeWhyBodyNoImport.description: Body of the first welcome section on a browser with no history API

welcomeSavedTitleNoImport.message: What it records as you browse
welcomeSavedTitleNoImport.description: Heading of the data section on a browser with no history API

welcomeSavedNoImportNote.message: From the first time you open a site, and never anything from before that.
welcomeSavedNoImportNote.description: Line under the recorded-data list on a browser with no history API

welcomeNotSavedTitle.description: Heading of the paragraph listing what is not stored

welcomeNotSaved.message: Page addresses, page titles, search queries and anything you have typed are not stored. Only the five things above, per host name.
welcomeNotSaved.description: What the import deliberately does not store

welcomeStorageTitle.description: Heading of the section about where the data lives

welcomeStorageBody.message: In this browser’s own storage, on this device. Visilant has no server and no account, and none of it is ever sent anywhere. You can erase all of it at any time in the settings.
welcomeStorageBody.description: Statement that the data stays on the device

welcomeOpenSettings.description: Label of the welcome page button opening the settings

welcomeDone.description: Label of the welcome page button closing the tab

welcomeDefaultsTitle.description: Heading of the section suggesting a look at the settings

welcomeDefaultsBody.message: The defaults are meant to suit most people, but they were picked by one person, largely around how that person browses. Visilant collects no telemetry – there is no way to see how anyone else has things set, and so no way to know what a better default would even be. Spend a couple of minutes in the settings: what warns you, when, and how loudly is all adjustable, and reading through it is also the fastest way to understand how the extension works.
welcomeDefaultsBody.description: Why the defaults are a guess and worth reviewing

emailMailSitesLabel.description: Label for the editable mapping of a mail domain to the site it is read on

emailMailSitesDesc.message: Nobody ever opens gmail.com – Gmail is read on mail.google.com – so an address domain collects no visits of its own. One mapping per line, as "gmail.com = mail.google.com". Well-known providers are mapped already, and lines here add to them.
emailMailSitesDesc.description: Explanation under the mail-site mapping field

emailMailSitesUpdateUrlLabel.description: Label for remote sources of the mail-site mapping

emailMailSitesUpdateUrlDesc.message: One URL per line, each a list of the same mapping lines. Empty by default – no public list of this kind exists, so this is here for anyone who keeps one.
emailMailSitesUpdateUrlDesc.description: Explanation under the remote mail-site source field

mailSiteLabel.description: Heading above the sites an address domain's mail is actually read on

mailSiteNote.message: An address domain is not a site anyone opens, so it never collects visits. The mail is read on the site above, and those visits are the ones worth reading.
mailSiteNote.description: Note under the mail-site list in the check panel

familiarityNoDatesTitle.message: Some sites are older than the browser remembers
familiarityNoDatesTitle.description: Title of the warning shown when a full import has run and dates are still missing

familiarityNoDatesText.message: sites have no active-day count and no first-visit date, and the browser history no longer reaches them – it does not go back that far, or it was cleared since. The full import has already run, so nothing can fill these in, and those two checks will keep failing for them. Only the visit count still speaks for these sites.
familiarityNoDatesText.description: Body of the warning shown when a full import has run and dates are still missing

familiarityNoImportTitle.message: Some sites were here before Visilant
familiarityNoImportTitle.description: Heading of the missing-dates card on a browser with no history API

familiarityNoImportText.message: sites have no active-day count and no first-visit date. This browser keeps its history to itself, so there is no import that could fill them in and those two checks will keep failing for them. Only the visit count still speaks for these sites. Everything you visit from now on records both from its first visit.
familiarityNoImportText.description: Body of the missing-dates card on a browser with no history API, such as Firefox for Android
